title: Graph homomorphism parameterized by both treewidths
area: Database theory and finite model theory
formal:
Do there exist one deterministic Turing-machine algorithm \(A\), a total computable function \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\), and an integer constant \(C\ge1\) such that, for every pair of explicitly given finite simple undirected graphs \(G,H\), \(A\) decides whether there is a graph homomorphism \(G\to H\) in at most
\[
f(k)(L+2)^C\quad\text{bit operations},\qquad
k=\max\{\operatorname{tw}(G),\operatorname{tw}(H)\},
\]
where \(L\) is the full binary encoding length? Both graphs vary with the input. The exponent \(C\) must be independent of \(k\), the vertex counts and both graphs.
why: Bounding the source graph alone permits dynamic programming whose exponent can depend on its treewidth. The question asks whether simultaneously controlling the target graph removes that dependence from the exponent, a basic structural tractability boundary for homomorphism and query evaluation.
status_note: Current status uncertain. The primary question author announced in May 2025 that a W[1]-hardness result was expected from workshop discussions, but the checked page gives neither the reduction nor its publication. This review fixes the user-selected graph target without presenting it as confidently open or archiving it from an unverified announcement.

sentences: Both inputs are finite simple undirected graphs, and the task is to decide whether one maps homomorphically into the other.
The parameter is the larger of the two treewidths.
The requested algorithm may depend arbitrarily and computably on that parameter, but its polynomial input-size exponent must be fixed.
Algorithms for one fixed target graph or with a width-dependent exponent do not meet the requirement.
A primary-source announcement of hardness makes current status uncertain until the supporting reduction is verified.

definitions:
A finite simple undirected graph has an explicitly listed vertex set \([n]\), possibly empty, and a set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Input encodings list vertices and edges in binary with delimiters and contain no loops, parallel edges, vertex colors, weights or allowed-image lists. Neither graph is fixed in advance. The length \(L\) includes both graphs. Polynomially equivalent standard explicit graph encodings give the same target.

A homomorphism is any function \(h:V(G)\to V(H)\) for which \(\{h(u),h(v)\}\in E(H)\) whenever \(\{u,v\}\in E(G)\). It need not be injective or surjective, and nonedges need not map to nonedges. The output is just the existence bit, not the number of maps or a list of them. There is one map from the empty graph to every graph and no map from a nonempty graph to the empty graph.

A tree decomposition of \(G\) consists of a finite nonempty tree \(T\) and bags \(B_t\subseteq V(G)\) such that every vertex appears in a bag, every edge has both endpoints together in some bag, and the nodes whose bags contain a given vertex form a connected subtree. Its width is \(\max(0,\max_t |B_t|-1)\). The treewidth is the minimum width of a tree decomposition, so it is zero for the empty graph and for edgeless graphs. The same definitions apply to \(H\). No tree decompositions, treewidth values or upper bounds are supplied to \(A\).

The algorithm must be uniform across all inputs and terminate with the correct decision. A total computable parameter function means a single finite program outputs \(f(k)\) on each nonnegative integer \(k\), with no efficiency bound on that auxiliary computation. The algorithm may incur arbitrarily large dependence on \(k\), but only a fixed polynomial exponent in the whole input length. This is the meaning of fixed-parameter tractability in this card. Running time counts ordinary finite binary operations, with no graph oracle or advice depending on input size.

An algorithm whose exponent grows with \(k\) does not meet the target, even if it is polynomial for every fixed \(k\). Likewise, a guarantee with arbitrary dependence on \(|V(G)|\), or a guarantee for one fixed target \(H\), is insufficient. A graph-isomorphism algorithm need not decide this homomorphism problem. The card selects the concrete graph formulation linked by the query-evaluation source, rather than all relational signatures and arities.

The displayed question is the literal existence statement. A hardness theorem relative to an unproved parameterized-complexity separation gives a conditional obstruction, which must be identified as conditional; it is not by itself an unconditional proof that every such algorithm fails.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed uniform algorithm-existence statement. An affirmative answer must provide the algorithm, a computable parameter bound and an exponent independent of the parameter. A purported unconditional negative answer must establish the full negation; a hardness classification under an unproved class separation must be labeled conditional rather than silently substituted for that negation.
